sentences.text: Nicrosaurus was an extinct genus of phytosaur reptile that closely resembled modern crocodiles but was not closely related to them, representing a striking example of parallel evolution.

Its skull featured external nares positioned directly in front of the forehead at the skull roof level, a broad heavy rostrum, and a strong prenarial crest, differing significantly from the snout-tip nostrils of crocodiles.
The name Nicrosaurus was possibly derived from the Neckar river in southwestern Germany, the region where these fossils were originally found.
Nicrosaurus nostrils were positioned directly in front of the forehead, similar to modern cetaceans, unlike crocodiles where they are at the snout tip.
Nicrosaurus had massive snouts similar to modern crocodilians, suggesting it preyed on tetrapods rather than fish.
An isolated Nicrosaurus tooth found in 2002 among fish scales suggests the animal may have lived in swampy areas or scavenged dead fish.
The genus Nicrosaurus was described by the German paleontologist Oscar Fraas in 1866.

Herbert E. Gregory originally assigned the species Rutiodon gregorii to the genus Nicrosaurus, but the species previously known as Phytosaurus gregorii was later reclassified as Nicrosaurus gregorii due to skull similarities.
The species Nicrosaurus kapffi was originally described by Meyer in 1860.
Nicrosaurus meyeri was described by Hungerbühler and Hunt in 2000.
Some skulls found in the Chinle Formation were incorrectly identified as Nicrosaurus rather than the genus Rutiodon.

Nicrosaurus was likely a secondarily terrestrial predator with a deep upper jaw and heterodont teeth, similar to terrestrial crocodylomorphs, and recent analysis of post-cranial bones supports the idea that it was primarily terrestrial.
The ilium and femur of Nicrosaurus resemble terrestrial archosaurs, suggesting it had an upright walking style.
Nicrosaurus kapffi likely had a mixed diet that included both fish and tetrapods based on microwear patterns on its teeth.
Nicrosaurus meyeri had dietary habits similar to N. kapffi, overlapping with carnivores, fish-eaters, and consumers of hard-shelled invertebrates.

Nicrosaurus buceros was distinguished from N. kapffi by having a narrower snout, while N. kapffi is characterized by a long snout, a ventrally convex alveolar rim of the maxilla, and a tripartite upper dentition, and N. meyeri is characterized by a very long snout and a bipartite upper dentition.

A 2002 study placed the genera Machaeroprosopus, Mystriosuchus, Redondasaurus, and Nicrosaurus within the clade Mystriosuchini, where Nicrosaurus is considered the most basal member and belongs to the parent group Mystriosuchini and the family Parasuchidae.
Nicrosaurus lived during the Late Triassic period, specifically the Norian to Rhaetian stages, from 227.3 to 201.4 million years ago.

Nicrosaurus fossils were found in arkosic sandstones and lacustrine sandstones, indicating a freshwater river habitat, with N. kapffi and N. meyeri fossils found in the Norian-aged Stubensandstein of southwestern Germany and the Norian Arnstadt Formation, a lake-based sedimentary sequence in the Germanic Basin, in environments associated with rivers, lakes, or dry floodplains.
Nicrosaurus specimens have been found in various rock types including sandstone, marl, dolomite, breccia, and claystone.
It was initially debated that phytosaurs were semi-aquatic with a fish-based diet due to their resemblance to modern crocodiles.

Scientific literature mentions two additional species, Nicrosaurus gregorii and Nicrosaurus buceros, beyond the two primary species, and the remains of Nicrosaurus gregorii and Nicrosaurus buceros were found in the Chama basin of north-central New Mexico.
